```{r setup, include=FALSE}
site <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = site,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
```

A two-part model is used when an outcome is the product of a mix of two
processes, one for observed zeroes and non-zeroes, and one for an amount among
the non-zeroes. The expected outcome is the product of the two:

$$E(y) = \Pr(y > 0) \times E(y \mid y > 0)$$

In R, fit the two parts as separate models and combine them with `suest()` and
the `twopart` option. Predictions and marginal effects from `marginaleffects` are then on
the expected outcome, with standard errors from the joint covariance of the
two parts.

The examples use the medical expenditures of 19,386 adults in the 2004 Medical
Expenditure Panel Survey. The first part is a logit of whether a person had any
medical expenditures. The second part is a Poisson model of expenditures among
the people who had any. With the robust standard errors `suest()` computes,
this is Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood: it fits a model of the mean of any
outcome that is zero or positive, not only counts, and needs only the model of
the mean to be right (Santos Silva and Tenreyro 2006). `family = quasipoisson`
fits it without warnings about outcomes that are not whole numbers.

## Fit the two parts and combine them

Both parts cluster on the dwelling unit (`duid`):

```{r fit}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)

meps <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/meps.dta"))
meps[c("female", "ins_unins", "anylim")] <-
  lapply(meps[c("female", "ins_unins", "anylim")], factor)
table(meps$exp_tot > 0)

any <- glm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
             anylim, family = binomial, data = meps)
amount <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
                anylim, family = quasipoisson, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)

fit <- suest(any, amount, model_names = c("Any", "Amount"), cluster = "duid",
             twopart = TRUE)
summary(fit)
```

With survey data, put the weights and clusters in a `svydesign()`, fit the
first part to the full design and the second part to the people with any
expenditures, and give `suest()` the full design. `wts = TRUE` averages with
the sampling weights:

```{r survey}
design <- survey::svydesign(ids = ~duid, weights = ~wtdper, data = meps)
any_s <- survey::svyglm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 +
                          ins_unins + anylim, design = design,
                        family = quasibinomial)
amount_s <- survey::svyglm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 +
                             ins_unins + anylim,
                           design = subset(design, exp_tot > 0),
                           family = quasipoisson)
fit_s <- suest(any_s, amount_s, survey_design = design,
               observation_id = "dupersid", twopart = TRUE)
avg_slopes(fit_s, variables = c("age", "ins_unins"), wts = TRUE)
```

## Expected expenditures and effects on them

Predictions are the product of the two parts: the probability of any
expenditures from `Any` times the expected expenditures of someone who has
any from `Amount`:

```{r effects}
avg_predictions(fit)
avg_slopes(fit, variables = c("age", "female", "ins_unins", "anylim"))
```

Expected expenditures average about $3,680 a year. Being uninsured is
associated with $2,700 less in expenditure; each year of age predicts a $49
increase; being female, a $417 increase; and having any activity limitation, a
$1,533 increase.

## Effects in each part

`type = "positive"` gives the effect on the probability of any expenditures,
and `type = "amount"` the effect on the expected expenditures of someone who
has any:

```{r parts}
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "positive")
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "amount")
```

Being uninsured lowers the probability of any expenditures by 24 percentage
points, and the expected expenditures of someone who has any by about $2,600.
Both are averaged over the whole sample, so the two effects are for the same
people. `newdata = subset(exp_tot > 0)` averages the amount effect over only
the people with any expenditures, the observations the second part was fit to:

```{r parts-positive}
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "amount",
                newdata = subset(exp_tot > 0))
```

Among the people with any expenditures, being uninsured is associated with
about $2,830 less in expenditure. This describes the people who spend, but it
is averaged over different observations than the first part's effect, so the
two can differ partly because the observations used to calculate the marginal
effect differ.

## How well the model predicts

The correlation between the outcome and its expected value summarizes how well
a two-part model predicts. It depends only on the expected outcome, so it
applies with any second part:

```{r fit-correlation}
p <- predictions(fit)
cor(p$exp_tot, p$estimate)
```

The correlation is .392.

## Other second parts

The second part can also be a Gamma model with a log link
(`glm(family = Gamma(link = "log"))`), a linear model (`lm()`), or a negative
binomial model (`MASS::glm.nb()`); `twopart` works the same way with each.
With a linear model of the log of the outcome, add `retransform = "duan"` for
Duan's (1983) smearing estimate or `retransform = "normal"` for the
normal-theory retransformation:

```{r log-outcome}
meps$ln_exp <- ifelse(meps$exp_tot > 0, log(meps$exp_tot), NA)
ln_amount <- lm(ln_exp ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
                  anylim, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)
fit_ln <- suest(any, ln_amount, model_names = c("Any", "LnAmount"),
                cluster = "duid", twopart = TRUE, retransform = "duan")
avg_slopes(fit_ln, variables = c("age", "ins_unins"))
```

## Comparing two-part models

This example compares two second parts: a Gamma model with a log link, and
Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood. Both share the first part, a logit of
whether a person had any expenditures. `twopart` names the two pairs, each a
first part and its second part; `Any` is in both:

```{r compare-fit}
any <- glm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
           family = binomial, data = meps)
gamma <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
             family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)
poisson <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
               family = quasipoisson, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)

fit2 <- suest(any, gamma, poisson, model_names = c("Any", "Gamma", "Poisson"),
              twopart = c("Any", "Gamma", "Any", "Poisson"))
effects2 <- avg_comparisons(fit2, variables = c("ins_unins", "age"))
effects2
hypotheses(effects2, hypothesis = difference ~ pairwise | term)
```

The two models give nearly the same effect of being uninsured: expected
expenditures about $2,840 lower. The difference between them, about $4, is not
significant. The effect of a year of age is about $108 with the Gamma second
part and $100 with the Poisson one, and that difference, about $8, is
significant.

A two-part model can also be compared with a single model for the outcome.
Models not named in `twopart` keep their own prediction -- here, a Poisson
model fit to everyone, zeros included:

```{r compare-one-part}
one_part <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
                family = quasipoisson, data = meps)

fit3 <- suest(any, poisson, one_part, model_names = c("Any", "Poisson", "OnePart"),
              twopart = c("Any", "Poisson"))
effects3 <- avg_comparisons(fit3, variables = c("ins_unins", "age"))
effects3
hypotheses(effects3, hypothesis = difference ~ pairwise | term)
```

The one-part model gives a larger effect of being uninsured, about $3,030, or
about $180 more than the two-part model, and the difference is significant.
The effects of age are close, about $100 and $101, though the difference of
about $1 is significant.
